content: Herpes simplex is a viral disease caused by herpes simplex viruses (HSV). Genital herpes is typically caused by HSV-2 and is most commonly transmitted through sexual contact. Oral herpes, often referred to as cold sores, is usually caused by HSV-1. Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause episodes of active disease, characterized by painful blisters containing infectious viral particles. These episodes typically last between 2 and 21 days and are followed by periods of remission when the sores heal. Many cases of genital herpes are asymptomatic, but viral shedding can still occur, allowing transmission to others. HSV-1 and HSV-2 are transmitted through direct contact with sores or bodily fluids from an infected individual. After the initial infection, the viruses migrate to sensory nerves, where they remain dormant as lifelong latent infections. HSV-1 typically resides in the trigeminal ganglia, which provide sensation to the lips, lower mouth, and neck, while HSV-2 resides in the lumbosacral ganglia, which supply sensation to the genitals, perineum, and upper legs. Reactivation of the virus can occur, leading to recurrent outbreaks in the area of the skin initially infected. Triggers for reactivation are not fully understood but may include sunburn, ultraviolet light, wind, trauma, surgery, and stress. Over time, the frequency of recurrences tends to decrease as the immune system develops specific immunity against the virus. HSV-2 is widespread, affecting approximately 1 in 4 females and 1 in 5 males in the United States. Among sexually active individuals with genital, anal, or perianal ulcers, genital herpes and syphilis are the most common causes, with genital herpes being the most prevalent. The frequency of these conditions varies by geographic region and population. Ocular herpes, typically caused by HSV-1, is a specific form of facial herpes infection known as herpes keratitis. It begins with infection of the epithelial cells on the surface of the eye and can involve retrograde infection of the nerves serving the cornea. Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is a severe and potentially life-threatening viral infection of the central nervous system. Neonatal HSV disease is a rare but serious condition, often resulting from vertical transmission of the virus from mother to newborn during delivery. Approximately 1 in 3,000 to 1 in 20,000 live births are affected by neonatal herpes. Around 22% of pregnant women have been previously exposed to HSV-2, and an additional 2% or more acquire the virus during pregnancy. Genital herpes infections caused by HSV-1 are increasingly common among young adults. Herpetic whitlow is a lesion on the finger or thumb caused by HSV. In children, the primary source of infection is the orofacial area, often resulting from finger-sucking or thumb-sucking, with HSV-1 being the most common cause. In adults, the primary source is often the genital region, with HSV-2 being more prevalent. Healthcare workers, such as dentists, are also at risk due to increased exposure to the virus. Herpes gladiatorum, also known as wrestler’s herpes or mat herpes, is caused by HSV-1 and occurs in individuals participating in contact sports like wrestling, rugby, and soccer. Abrasions in the skin provide an entry point for the virus. Symptoms typically appear within two weeks of direct skin-to-skin contact with an infected person and include skin ulceration on the face, ears, and neck, as well as fever, headache, sore throat, and swollen glands. Recurrences of physical symptoms may occur. Mollaret’s meningitis is a recurrent, benign, aseptic meningitis caused by HSV. It involves inflammation of the protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord (the meninges). HSV-1 and HSV-2 can be shed from sores caused by the viruses, but they can also be released from skin that appears normal between outbreaks. HSV-2 is primarily transmitted through sexual contact with an infected individual, even if they do not have visible sores or are unaware of their infection. HSV-1 can cause genital herpes through oral-genital or genital-genital contact. Genital HSV-1 outbreaks tend to recur less frequently than genital HSV-2 outbreaks. The most effective way to prevent genital herpes transmission is to abstain from sexual contact or to engage in a long-term mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who has been tested and is known to be uninfected. Latex condoms can reduce the risk of transmission but do not provide complete protection, as genital ulcer diseases can occur in areas not covered by condoms. Individuals with herpes should avoid sexual activity with uninfected partners when lesions or other symptoms are present. Asymptomatic individuals can still transmit the virus to sexual partners. The prevalence of HSV-1 and HSV-2 infections varies globally. Socioeconomic status is a significant factor, with higher levels of HSV-1 infection and earlier acquisition rates observed in developing countries compared to industrialized nations. Risk factors for acquiring HSV-2 include being female, being Black, becoming sexually active at a young age, having multiple sexual partners, and lower socioeconomic status. Asymptomatic shedding of HSV occurs in most infected individuals. Genital herpes can cause recurrent painful genital sores in many adults and can be severe in immunocompromised patients. Pregnant women should avoid contracting herpes during pregnancy, as a newly acquired infection in late pregnancy increases the risk of transmission to the baby. If a woman has active genital herpes at the time of delivery, a cesarean section is usually recommended. Herpes infection increases susceptibility to HIV, potentially contributing to the spread of HIV. If left untreated, herpes simplex can become recurrent. Neonatal herpes infection is a rapidly progressive disease that can lead to central nervous system (CNS) involvement and disseminated disease. Early diagnosis and treatment with acyclovir can prevent disease progression. Untreated infections can rarely progress to involve the CNS and other organ systems, presenting with symptoms such as irritability, confusion, and respiratory difficulty. Disseminated disease may occur in rare cases, and CNS involvement can result in residual neurological deficits. Other complications include pneumonia, esophagitis, encephalitis, premature birth, spontaneous abortion, and infant death. The prognosis for herpes skin infections in immunocompetent individuals is generally good. The use of acyclovir has reduced mortality in CNS and disseminated disease, but the prognosis remains poor in immunocompromised individuals and infants. Primary orofacial herpes caused by HSV-1 presents as multiple, round, superficial oral ulcers. Adults with atypical presentations are more challenging to diagnose. Prodromal symptoms that occur before the appearance of herpetic lesions can help differentiate HSV from other conditions with similar symptoms, such as allergic stomatitis. Genital herpes is more difficult to diagnose than oral herpes, as most individuals with genital HSV-2 infection do not exhibit classic signs and symptoms. They may present with blisters and ulcers in the genital area similar to orofacial herpes. Herpes infections can recur even after successful initial treatment. The first episode is usually longer, more painful, and more severe than subsequent episodes. On physical examination, multiple, round, superficial oral ulcers accompanied by acute gingivitis may be observed. Lymphadenopathy, gingivitis, and tonsillitis may also accompany primary lesions. Confirmation and characterization of HSV infection and its type through direct detection in genital lesions are essential for diagnosis, prognosis, counseling, and management. Cell culture and PCR are the preferred tests for individuals seeking medical treatment for genital ulcers or other mucocutaneous lesions. PCR assays for HSV DNA are more sensitive and are increasingly used in many settings. PCR is the test of choice for detecting HSV in spinal fluid for diagnosing CNS infections. Viral culture isolates should be typed to determine the specific HSV type causing the infection. Failure to detect HSV by culture or PCR does not rule out infection, as viral shedding is intermittent. Treatments are available to reduce symptoms and speed up the healing process of herpes infections, but there is currently no cure. Antiviral medications, such as acyclovir and valacyclovir, can shorten and prevent outbreaks while being taken. Daily suppressive therapy for symptomatic herpes can reduce transmission to partners. Some topical creams, such as docosanol and tromantadine, prevent the virus from entering the skin. Other drugs, such as cimetidine and probenecid, can reduce acyclovir clearance, and aspirin can reduce inflammation associated with viral infection. Some natural remedies may have potential benefits in reducing herpes outbreaks or their symptoms. No vaccine is currently available to prevent or treat herpes. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) in the United States is conducting phase III trials of a vaccine against HSV-2 called Herpevac. The vaccine has shown effectiveness only in women who have never been exposed to HSV-1. It is approximately 48% effective in preventing HSV-2 seropositivity and about 78% effective in preventing symptomatic HSV-2. However, the vaccine did not show efficacy in preventing HSV-2 in males during initial trials. Additionally, the vaccine only reduced the acquisition of HSV-2 and symptoms in women who were not infected with HSV-2 at the time of vaccination. Given that about 20% of individuals in the United States have HSV-2 infection, this limits the population for whom the vaccine might be appropriate. Since there is no cure for herpes, some individuals experience negative emotions following diagnosis, particularly if they have acquired the genital form of the disease. These feelings, which may include depression, fear of rejection, isolation, and self-destructive thoughts, often lessen over time. Support groups in the United States and the UK provide communities and information for individuals with herpes. Many people with herpes are hesitant to disclose their infection to others, including friends, family, and potential sexual partners. Some choose to disclose their status upfront, while others wait until a sexual relationship becomes likely. Others may choose to date only individuals who also have herpes.
